sec1.lens: Module 2 is where we frame the house — the Curiosity Headline is the door, the 3 Secrets are the walls, and the Offer is the foundation that holds it all up.
emphasis: The Offer is NOT a slide you polish at the end — it's the foundation you build the entire presentation on top of
Before you write a single headline, your offer stack and deliverables (video trainings, worksheets, the actual stuff) have to exist
The first three slides — Curiosity Headline, 3 Secrets, The Offer — are the skeleton of every webinar I've ever made $100M+ with
If you try to fix a weak offer with a stronger hook, you're putting a beautiful door on a house with no floor
common_traps: Skipping the prework and trying to write the hook before the offer is even built — you'll end up rewriting everything
Treating the three slides as equal when the Offer is load-bearing and the other two serve it
Making the Curiosity Headline about YOU instead of the result they want without the pain
Building fancy training content before nailing the core framework — going HOW before WHAT
voice_notes: 'The Offer is the foundation of the house — if it's right, everything else falls into place'
'Your First Three Slides — this is the skeleton'
'If you're struggling with your framework, go watch Course Secrets — I built that exactly for this moment'
'What is the Big Domino? The ONE belief that, if it falls, every other objection becomes irrelevant'

sec2.lens: This is where we stack the offer so it chains — every element solves one problem AND creates the next — until the final piece closes the loop with zero new problems.
emphasis: 'Solve One, Create One' is THE pattern that turned ClickFunnels into a $100M+ offer — traffic creates the funnel problem, funnel creates the software problem, software creates the course problem, course creates the copywriting problem
The final element MUST NOT introduce a new problem — if it does, your buyer walks out feeling incomplete and won't pull the trigger
Tie it to a timeline — 'six-pack abs in six weeks' — because buyers need to PROJECT themselves into the future with the result
The timeline is how you turn an overwhelming stack into an achievable path — same stack, reframed as a week-by-week journey
COMPLETE vs OVERWHELMING — those are the two emotions you're engineering against
common_traps: Stacking bonuses that don't chain — just a pile of stuff they'll never use — instead of a logical problem-solution sequence
The final element introducing a ghost problem (now what? how do I scale? what about taxes?) that kills the close
No timeline = no ROI picture in the buyer's head = they can't project themselves winning
Making the stack TOO complete — 12 elements when 6 would feel more achievable. More isn't better, the right sequence is better
Forgetting that COMPLETE and OVERWHELMING are opposites on the same dial — you're tuning that dial
voice_notes: 'Each element solves one problem but creates the next — that's the chain'
'Does your whole offer stack make them FEEL complete?'
'Think six-pack abs in six weeks — can they project themselves into the future having the result?'
'The last element cannot leave them with a new problem — if it does, you lose the sale'
'We did this exact thing with ClickFunnels — funnel, software, course, copywriting — each one solved the problem the last one created'

sec3.lens: You are TOO CLOSE to your own offer — the 2-3 minute breakout pitch is the stress test that exposes what your ego can't see.
emphasis: If you can't pitch the offer in 2-3 minutes without it feeling overwhelming, it IS overwhelming
Peer feedback catches the blind spots — you've been staring at this for weeks, they hear it fresh
The verbal pitch test is different from the written test — if it doesn't land when you SAY it, it won't land when you SELL it
This isn't optional — every top webinar I've ever built got torn apart in a room before it ever made a dollar
common_traps: Skipping the breakout because 'I already know my offer' — that's exactly the mindset that kills webinars
Pitching for 6-8 minutes instead of 2-3 because you can't kill your darlings
Taking feedback personally instead of treating it as free QA on a six-figure presentation
Using industry jargon in the pitch — if your peer doesn't get it, neither will your cold audience
voice_notes: 'You're too close to this — your peers aren't'
'If it feels overwhelming to them, it'll feel overwhelming to your buyer'
'Two to three minutes. If you can't do it that fast, you don't own your offer yet'

sec4.lens: This is the money slide — the Big Domino Statement and the Curiosity Headline together are what get the right person into the room AND prime them to believe ONE thing by the end.
emphasis: The Big Domino is the SINGLE point of belief — if this one domino falls, every other objection falls behind it
Jason Fladlien nailed it — one belief, emphasized from a variety of different angles, over and over — that's the whole game

The Big Domino Statement template is not optional — fill in the blanks EXACTLY: 'If I can make them believe that (new opportunity) is the key to (what they desire most) and is only attainable through (my specific vehicle) then all other objections become irrelevant and they HAVE to give me money'
Curiosity Headline = 'How To (result) Without (pain)' — that's the hook that gets them in the house
10 variations is the minimum — most people stop at 3 and pick a weak one
The headline lives on THREE places: registration page, title slide, and the lead-in to your origin story — consistency compounds belief
common_traps: Writing a Big Domino that's actually 3 beliefs in a trench coat — ONE point of belief, not three
Picking the 'new opportunity' that's really the same old opportunity rebranded — if it's not genuinely new, the domino won't fall
Curiosity Headlines that emphasize the HOW instead of the WITHOUT — the pain removed is what sells
Stopping at 3 headline variations when variation #8 is usually the winner
Making the headline clever instead of clear — cleverness is ego, clarity converts
voice_notes: 'What is the ONE thing they have to believe for everything else to be irrelevant?'
'Fladlien said it best — a single point of belief, emphasized from a variety of different angles, over and over'
'If I can make them believe that X is the key to Y and is only attainable through Z — they HAVE to give me money'
'How To... Without... — that's the formula. Result without the pain'
'Write 10 variations. Then write 10 more. The winner is almost never the first one'
'This is the hook that gets them into the house'

sec5.lens: Speak the Big Domino out loud — if it doesn't land in a breakout room with peers, it won't land with 500 strangers on a registration page.
emphasis: The spoken test catches what the written test can't — rhythm, punch, emotional weight
Let your peers rank your 10 variations — the one YOU love is rarely the one that pulls hardest
Capture every piece of feedback — even the notes you disagree with tell you something about where the hook is weak
This round is about the HOOK specifically — not the offer, not the framework, just the door to the house
common_traps: Defending your headline in the breakout instead of listening — you're not selling to your peers, you're stress-testing
Only getting positive feedback because you phrased the ask as 'does this sound good?' instead of 'which one pulls hardest?'
Refusing to kill your favorite variation when the room points at a different winner
voice_notes: 'Read it out loud. Does it LAND?'
'The one you love is rarely the one that pulls hardest'
'Let the room pick the winner'

sec6.lens: The 3 Secrets are the three angles that knock down the Big Domino from three sides — Vehicle, Internal, External — because if any ONE of those false beliefs survives, the sale doesn't close.
emphasis: Three false beliefs, three secrets — this is NOT arbitrary. Every audience holds these exact three categories of doubt
Secret #1 = Vehicle belief ('does this new opportunity actually work?') — prove the thing itself
Secret #2 = Internal belief ('can I personally do this?') — prove THEY can do it
Secret #3 = External belief ('will outside forces block me even if the vehicle and I are fine?') — prove the world won't stop them
It doesn't have to literally be 'Secrets' — could be 3 Myths, 3 Lies, 3 Questions — pick the framing that fits your audience energy
Each secret is a different ANGLE on the same Big Domino — Fladlien's principle. One belief, three angles
My Funnel Hacking example: Secret 1 (study funnels ethically), Secret 2 (clone in 10 min), Secret 3 (steal their traffic) — Vehicle / Internal / External, done
common_traps: Picking 3 secrets that are all addressing the Vehicle and ignoring Internal + External — the domino doesn't fall because two beliefs survive
Making the 3 Secrets into 3 different Big Dominos instead of 3 angles on ONE domino — now you're trying to sell 3 things and selling zero
Using 'Secrets' when your audience would respond harder to 'Myths' or 'Lies' — the packaging matters
Weak secret headlines that read like Table of Contents entries — these are mini-hooks, they need their own curiosity pull
Forgetting the Fladlien principle and treating the secrets as independent teaching modules instead of belief-shift assaults
voice_notes: 'Three Secrets, three angles, one Big Domino'
'Vehicle, Internal, External — if any one of those beliefs survives, the sale dies'
'It doesn't have to be Secrets — could be 3 Myths, 3 Lies, 3 Questions. Pick what your audience leans into'
'Can they do it? Will the world let them? Does the thing itself work? Those are the three doors you're knocking down'
'My 3 Secrets of Funnel Hacking — that literally built ClickFunnels into a billion-dollar company'

sec7.lens: Pressure-test the 3 Secret headlines in the breakout — each one needs to clearly map to Vehicle, Internal, or External, and each one needs to pull curiosity on its own.
emphasis: Ask peers 'which false belief does each secret address?' — if they can't answer cleanly, the mapping is off
The weakest Secret is the one to rewrite first — most people try to polish their favorite instead
Headlines that can't stand alone as curiosity hooks won't survive once they're announced during the webinar
common_traps: Asking 'do these sound good?' instead of 'can you tell me which belief each one addresses?'
Defending a weak Secret because you like the teaching content behind it — rewrite the headline, keep the content
Ignoring peer confusion about belief mapping — if they're confused, your audience will be too
voice_notes: 'Which false belief does each Secret address? If they can't tell you, rewrite it'
'The weakest one is the one you rewrite first — not your favorite'

sec8.lens: Next week we build the first 30 minutes — Framework Origin Story (how YOU discovered this, not your life story) + the Framework itself (WHAT, not HOW) — because the origin story is the Epiphany Bridge that makes them feel what you felt when you discovered it.
emphasis: CRITICAL distinction: Framework Origin Story is NOT your personal origin story — it's the story of how you discovered THIS specific framework / new opportunity
First 15 minutes = origin story (emotional setup). Next 15 minutes = framework (logical payoff). That's the 30-minute spine
WHAT not HOW — this is the Hero's Two Journeys principle. You teach the WHAT, the paid product delivers the HOW
If you teach the HOW on the webinar, there's nothing left to buy
Brainstorm with the community and coaches — the origin story you think is boring is often the one that converts (because it's authentic and specific)
The origin story creates the Epiphany Bridge — they feel the 'aha' moment YOU felt, and that's what makes them BELIEVE
common_traps: Telling your personal life story instead of the framework discovery story — nobody bought ClickFunnels because of my childhood, they bought it because of how I discovered the funnel hacking principle
Teaching the HOW on the webinar — now there's nothing left to sell
Skipping the origin story and jumping straight to the framework — you just handed them logic with no emotional trigger
Making the framework steps so granular it becomes a course inside the webinar — WHAT not HOW, high-level steps only
Winging the origin story without brainstorming — the best version is almost never your first version
voice_notes: 'Framework Origin Story — NOT your personal origin story. How did you come up with this new opportunity?'
'WHAT, not HOW. The webinar teaches WHAT. The product teaches HOW'
'First 15 minutes origin story, next 15 minutes framework. That's your first 30'
'The origin story is your Epiphany Bridge — they feel what you felt'
'Hero's Two Journeys — you take them on the emotional journey so they take themselves on the logical one'
'Brainstorm this with your community — the version you think is boring is usually the one that converts'
